oe1bu9454-226.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Blizanow to the Prince, answering his letter with its enclosures. Neither his first messenger, nor Sommer, nor General Schimmelpfennig has arrived, so he thinks the exchange plan with Schimmelpfennig has failed. He sends by express a letter from Graf Wartensleben about settling with Stössel and Weigel through the estates in the Duchy of Warsaw. He defends himself at length against the Prince's reproach about the lawsuits and the missing money. The Prefect wants the original deed for the Zagórów estates, or the estates will be confiscated. He asks whether the Trąbczyn lawsuit should go on.

oe1bu9454-227.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Blizanow to the Prince. He sends on Brzechffa's offer to lease the Zagórów estate for 6 years, with its terms. He advises signing a contract because war is coming and he cannot raise the taxes and interest; he lists five payments that are due. The arrests have been lifted, but sequestration will return if the costs stay unpaid. Brzechffa is taking over the collection of interest and arrears. Triebenfeld asks the Prince to choose: deal with Schimmelpfennig, or lease to Brzechffa and then settle with Weigel and Stössel to free Koschentin. He also reports new taxes from the Warsaw Reichstag and sends New Year wishes. Nothing in the letter concerns Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-228.notes: Promemoria signed "Sommer", written at Schlawenschitz to "Ew Durchleucht" (recipient given as not identified). It reports on his mission to General Schimmelpfennig v der Oye about the planned exchange involving the Zagórów estates. The General is still willing, but two things have slowed the matter: his illness, and his son's negotiations with Stägemann in Berlin over money that is to be released. Those negotiations have improved since the Saxon envoy stepped in. Because it is winter the estates cannot be inspected, so the General asks for the matter to be put off until spring. Two passages are garbled (lines 15-16 and 24-25).

claims.statement: Das Promemoria ist von Sommer unterzeichnet und berichtet über seine Sendung zu General Schimmelpfennig v der Oye.
Der General ist weiter bereit, den geplanten Tausch mit den Zagórówer Gütern einzugehen.
Verzögert haben ihn seine Krankheit und die Verhandlungen seines Sohnes mit Stägemann in Berlin über die herauszugebenden Gelder.
Durch Vermittlung des sächsischen Gesandten, an den sich der Rittmeister v Schimmelpfennig wandte, stehen diese Verhandlungen nun günstiger.
Wegen des Winters ist keine Besichtigung der Güter möglich, und der General bittet, die Sache bis zum Frühjahr auszusetzen.

oe1bu9454-229.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Blizanow to the Prince with birthday wishes. He passes on thanks from Graf Lipski, Smogorzewski and the tribunal councillors for game the Prince sent, and expects this to show in the Oleśnica and "Wrąbczyn" cases. He has made a lease contract for the Zagórów estates with Brzechffa at 20000 rt, subject to the Prince's approval, and plans to arrive in Schlawenschitz on 8 Feb so it can be concluded there. The interest is secured and the Bayonne capital will be paid off. The documents the Prince sent have been handed in, the dispute is settled and taxes may be reduced. The originals will be returned. A "Parobeck" is coming, perhaps with a bigger dog.

oe1bu9454-230.notes: This is a draft or set of fragments from Prince Hohenlohe to Triebenfeld. (1) Lines 2-54: he complains that Triebenfeld missed his own date, the 8th, for coming with Brzechffa. The Prince gets nothing from the estates and his son is arriving soon. General von Schimmelpfennig wants to acquire Zagórów and will view it in early March. The Prince asks for a definite answer and for money. (2) Lines 55-83: a fragment. Someone ("p Sommer", line 71) is being sent to confer openly with Triebenfeld or to come back with him. The Prince wants exact knowledge of the estates because of a "Commission". (3) Lines 84-115: his letter of the 19th of the previous month went unanswered. He asks for the deed of gift ("Trapergner", garbled) and for a plan for Zagórów. He does not object to leasing to Brzechffa but urges haste, because he has asked the King for a commission to settle his debts.

oe1bu9454-231.notes: C. F. Weigel writes from Breslau to Triebenfeld. He wants to discuss and consult on the affairs between the Prince of Hohenlohe and himself, and asks Triebenfeld to name a day for a meeting in Kalisz or wherever he prefers. He plans a Warsaw trip with Brzechffa about the Trąbczyn and Wrąbczyn matters. The 300 rt for Sommer cannot be found. He asks for a court-certified declaration assigning him 3125 rt (4219 rt with interest and costs) from the dues of several villages. He describes the want caused by troops. The Prince has written "Jawohl!" in the margin. Much of the text is garbled.

oe1bu9454-237.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Kalisz to the Prince. His last letter went via Amtmann König, who posted it in Polnisch Wartenberg rather than sending it by express to Schlawenschitz. He must leave tonight for Dresden because his eldest son lies in Naumburg, shot through both thighs. He will be back in Dresden within 12 days and asks for the Prince's letter to be sent there to wait at the post office. Once he has the Prince's letter to the Emperor, he expects to get Trąbczyn and Kaemen back. He has not seen Trzciński, König, Zerboni or Meierowitz and gets only evasions. oe1bu9454-240.notes: Triebenfeld writes to the Prince from Neustadt during the 1813 armistice. It is a political and military report: Austria stays neutral; the Russian troops and generals grumble about the armistice; there is a reported exchange in which Köckritz quarrels with Hardenberg in front of the monarch; supplying the troops is a problem; Zastrow will command the Landwehr gathering at Neisse; General Ortel is ill. Triebenfeld plans to travel via Neisse to Frankenstein, then to the headquarters, then to Schweinern to bring in produce and raise money. Nothing about Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-242.notes: Triebenfeld writes to the Prince from Vienna. He describes the journey, the high prices and the paper money. The Congress is postponed to 1 November and the sovereigns are going to Ofen and Pest. France resists the Saxon and Polish acquisitions, but Hardenberg stands firm. Württemberg affairs go well: the King will draft a constitution. He mentions Metternich, the marriage, Gärtner and Goesch. He discussed the Schlawenschitz affair with Barbe and A. and submitted his plan to Hardenberg. Koschentin must wait until the Curische Sache succeeds. Nothing can be decided on Kulm, Kaemen or Trąbczyn before Poland's fate is settled. The Moscinska née Prusimska has great friends. PS: princes unable to provide 12000 men are to be mediatised.

oe1bu9454-243.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna to the Prince, asking for money. Prices are very high. He had to change 400 rt, because Prussian Courant is not accepted, and got 1200 fl Wiener Einlösungsscheine. He has spent 392 fl and has about 800 fl left. He lists his daily costs: about 45 fl 30 x, so he reckons 50 fl W.W., or 15 rt, a day. After setting aside 260 fl for the return journey and other costs, he could live for about 10 days, but the business is expected to last at least 5 more weeks. He asks for 300 rt in gold; without it he will leave on the 23rd. He gives his address. Nothing on Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-249.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna during the Congress to the Prince. He acknowledges two letters. oe1bu9454-253.notes: Triebenfeld, in Vienna, writes to the Prince. He handed Hoffrath Hahn's latest opinion to the Staats Kanzler, who replied that it adds nothing new but agrees with the earlier view. The Staats Kanzler's quoted answer goes on: the Herzogin von Sagan seeks the King's leave to raise money on Sagan and pledges what the King owes her, which is the sum guaranteed for Fürst Hohenlohe; the King has postponed the matter. Triebenfeld wants written assurance before concluding with the Curische Mandatarien. On Trąbczyn and Kaemen he got a curt answer (enclosed, cf. doc 252) and concludes the matter will be settled in the general settlement. Also political news: the King of Württemberg threatens to leave, and there is unrest in Württemberg, Baden and Switzerland.

oe1bu9454-254.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna during the Congress, probably November 1814. He complains that no answers or money reach him. He is in debt to Barbe and demands more funds. He lists what his efforts will achieve: the Polish estates recovered, the Curische debt of 461000 rt paid off, compensation, and release from Koszęcin. He asks that letters go via Neisse under cover to Ober Post Direktor Mann. He warns against talking early about the Koszęcin sale. Enclosures: a) a receipt for 60 Fr d'or from Carl; b) a receipt for 50 Fr d'or from Bally, Breslau, 2 May 1809; c) a plea to send 200 rt to his daughter and 100 # to him.

oe1bu9454-256.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna during the Congress. The monarchs' departure is put off by 4 to 6 weeks, so nothing on the Polish estates can be settled yet. The main matter, the settlement with the Curish heirs and the advance of 112/m rt, is still open. He complains that he has no money, instructions or files: the 1811 Transact is incomplete, and he has never seen the other Transacte or the Codizill. He distrusts Stägemann, asks for proofs and blanks, asks the Prince to support his children in Breslau and to detain his bad servant.

oe1bu9454-259.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna to Prince Friedrich Ludwig. He expects any minute Staatskanzler Hardenberg's resolution telling the Brieg Oberlandesgericht to investigate the matter at once and report. If the court's report agrees with Triebenfeld's submissions, Hardenberg will have 112/m rt paid. He tells the Prince to declare everything openly before the commissioner (Brieg or Schlawenschitz): he was induced to join the transacts, the debts are fictitious, Cosmar forged everything, the papers were sent to Öhringen while he was under arrest. He should consult Hoffrath Hahn and spare nobody, not even his son. The news goes by courier to Neisse and on by estafette. Barbe, Gärtner and Göschel are helping. The congress's end is not in sight. Nothing on Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-260.notes: Triebenfeld in Vienna to Prince Hohenlohe. Yesterday he sent Hardenberg's resolution and the order to the Brieg Oberlandesgericht by estafette via Neisse. He relies on Hoffrath Hahn. He sets out seven points for the Prince's declaration (induced into the Transacte/Codizill while in custody, fictitious sums, Cosmar's schemes, the son turned against his father) and the aim: annul the Transacte against the 1799 document, leave the estates to the Prince, settle with the creditors, advance 112/m rt. He stays in Vienna until the Brieg matter and Poland are settled. He asks for a copy, blank sheets (Blanquets) and a thank-you letter to Hardenberg. Postscript: Humboldt is helping; he urgently needs 300 rt in gold and has only 118 fl left.

Triebenfeld hopes that, together with Eberhard, they can settle with the Curische Erben. He fears a misunderstanding, because the Fürst Kanzler wants the Prince heard in person, either in Brieg or by a commissioner sent to Schlawenschitz, who is to report back to him. The Polish question stays at rest until the Congress ends. New Year wishes. Nothing on Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-264.notes: Triebenfeld writes to the Prince about the Koszęcin (Koschentin) affair and asks him to keep it strictly secret. He touched on it with Hardenberg and got a short answer, and he heard that the King will no longer allow estates to be exchanged or bought. He then told Barbe the plan, including the 30000 Rthl present said to have been demanded for Hardenberg. Barbe was outraged and was only calmed when shown the Prince's signed instruction. Now Graf Pourtalès, who wants to buy estates in Silesia, is to buy Koszęcin, with Barbe acting as go-between. Triebenfeld has promised Barbe 30000 Rthl. He asks the Prince to send the draft Revers (lines 68-78), made out for the Prince's signature. Lines 55 and 57 are garbled. Nothing concerns Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-265a.notes: The letter is dated Schlawenschitz, 8 January 1815. Sender and recipient are not identified. It is addressed to a "Geheimer Staats Rath" and speaks of Majorats Güter, the writer's sons and Cosmar, but no names can be added. The writer thanks the addressee for steering his affairs, which Triebenfeld reports, with the hope of rescue from Cosmar. He refers to a report of the Oberlandesgericht at Brieg and asks for a state advance of 112/m Rthl to pay off heirs. He explains how the advance could be repaid from funds Cosmar must account for. Several words are garbled (Burischen, Garischer, 11213., the passage on 461000). Nothing concerns Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-265b.notes: The estate owner, not named in the document, writes from Schlawenschitz to a "Herr General", also unnamed. The late King granted him the confiscated Prusimski estates of Kamionna and Trąbczyn in 1796. In 1807 the administrative commission took them away and gave them to Prusimski's daughter, now Moscinska. The Kalisz tribunal declined to act and referred him to Napoleon. Hardenberg told Triebenfeld to wait until Poland's affairs were settled. Now the Prosna is said to be the border, so the Trąbczyn district falls to the Emperor, apparently of Russia (the word is garbled). The writer fears Moscinski's influence on the Governor-General. He asks the General to use his influence with the Emperor to get the estates back with 8 years' revenues, and to receive Triebenfeld.

oe1bu9454-266.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna during the Congress. Russia is demanding the Prosna as the border, which would put Trąbczyn and his own Blizanów estates under Russian rule. The Fürst Kanzler opposes this. If Russia gets the districts, the matter must be settled with Kaiser Alexander; Dąbska/Moscinska is in favour with Lanskoy. He is waiting for the Brieg Oberlandesgericht report. He gives the route for letters (cover to Barbe, via Post Director Balke in Dresden) and has had nothing since 17 Dec. He wants the blanquets, powers of attorney, the letter to the Kanzler and the Revers for Barbe. Pourtalès is likely to take part. He owes Barbe 104 ducats and asks for 100 and then 200 more.

The Staatskanzler forbids him any démarche. Moscinski (husband of the née Prusimska) and Graf Lanskoy are close friends. Rumours about Saxony, Wellington, Metternich and Talleyrand. The Majorat matter lies with Stägemann. If the creditors are satisfied, Cosmar's arrest on the estates will be lifted. He is shocked by the revenue estimate attached to the Brieg protocol. oe1bu9454-272.notes: Hoffrath Hahn writes to Prince Friedrich Ludwig, sending the draft reply to Fürst August he was ordered to write. He thinks the withdrawal of the Vollmacht follows from the Vienna decisions. He fears new blunders in Öhringen that could only be averted by talking in person, and asks for a secret instruction and a power of attorney for the worst case. He hopes the Prince will add something in his own hand about the travel money. He blames H. v. Braun, who was no match for Cosmar. He plans to inspect the estates to show their true yield and building needs, and to propose a fund. He wants the estates' means kept from a Berlin advocate. Nothing on Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-274.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna, where he is ill, to the Prince with news from the Congress. The King of Württemberg has called a Landtag for 15 March, and the princely houses have protested at the Congress. Barbe and Göschel ask that Fürst August be warned. There is also news on Saxony, Hessen-Darmstadt, East Frisia and Swedish Pomerania. The loan of 112000 rt was delayed by fear of war. On the Trąbczyn Vindication there is still no resolution from the Fürst Kanzler. A commission under General Amstetten exists, but he was advised against submitting to it yet. The deeds have been copied and certified and the court files translated. The Congress should last 6 more weeks, and Bülow is ill. Many words are garbled.

oe1bu9454-275.notes: Triebenfeld, sick in bed in Vienna, to the Prince. Stägemann has still made no report to the Staats Kanzler. Triebenfeld suspects ill will: the case would go Cosmar's way if the Brieg report were not so favourable to the Prince. He has been assured that the Fürst means well by the Hohenlohe houses, and something is going off to the King of Württemberg today; an enclosure is mentioned. His main worry is submitting the documents on Trąbczyn, Kulm and Kaemen to the Commission. The translator won't release the files until paid, and Triebenfeld has no money. He asks for money and the offered Blanquets. The closing political news is vague and figurative.

oe1bu9454-276.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna to Prince Hohenlohe. The Curische Erben matter: Justizcommissarius Eberhard (Brieg) sent disturbing news, enclosed. Triebenfeld has asked only for 112000 rt and for administration of the estates under the Prince's aegis. He urges that Eberhard be sent to Vienna to settle with the princesses. He explains that the King's answer to the three ladies was a political move drafted by Humboldt. Congress news: the King of Saxony is in Pressburg, and the monarchs' travel plans. The petition about the Polish estates is ready but needs the Chancellor's order and money for translations. Nothing about Trąbczyn specifically.

oe1bu9454-277.notes: Triebenfeld, in Wien, writes to the Prince. He has received the Prince's letter of the 6th by Estaffette, with a money order for 200 # and 3 blank signed sheets (Blanquets). He is ill and writing in haste. He wants Eberhard and Hahn to come to Wien. Stägemann has still not presented the matter. He has handed the Polish estates matter over again with all the files, and on Beguelin's advice he wrote to Zerboni (answer enclosed). Cosmar is said to be as good as ruined. August must take back his Vollmacht from the advocate. Bartenstein, Göschel and Winzingerode are pressing August. Pourtalès has not answered yet but is expected. Political news: Napoleon's escape and landing at Antibes, Murat, the King of Saxony. Encloses the King of Württemberg's papers concerning the Hohenlohe houses.

oe1bu9454-279.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna to Prince Friedrich Ludwig. What matters now is a real settlement (Vergleich) with the Curische heiresses. Once it is made, the Staats Kanzler will arrange the advance and the administration. He waits anxiously for Eberhard. Hohenlohe-Bartenstein, Winzingerode and Göschel have written to Langenburg and Kirchberg, and he expects Fürst August to have recalled the Vollmacht, which would leave Cosmar exposed. On the Polish estates the Kanzler asks for patience until the question of the Donatarien estates is settled. Most of the letter is Congress and Napoleon news. Nothing on Trąbczyn. Some garbled passages (Pourtalès, the kohl matter).

oe1bu9454-283.notes: A short French letter from Beguelin in Vienna to Prince Hohenlohe-Ingelfingen. He will soon hand the Prince's letter to the Prince Chancellier d'Etat (the Staats Kanzler; the letter gives no name) and will put the Prince's wishes before him. He would be glad to be the Chancellor's instrument in meeting those wishes. He had not known Triebenfeld before and met him only in Vienna. Triebenfeld's mention of the Prince was enough for him to pay full attention. Nothing about Trąbczyn. The text is sound, and the period French spelling (assés, connoitre, daignée) is left as it is.

oe1bu9454-284.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna to the Prince. The outbreak of war is holding everything up. Trąbczyn, Kamionna and Kolno will not come back to the Prince: Alexander got "unsern Allgsten Herren" to sign that the Poles keep the estates the commission returned to them. Triebenfeld is therefore petitioning for compensation and sets out his calculation. Kamionna: 93000 rt in cash plus 120000 rt in estates. Trąbczyn: valued at 316000 rt, net 246000 rt after debts. Total 459000 rt: 366000 rt in debt-free estates plus 93000 rt in cash. Weigel's 30000 rt have been moved onto Zagorowo. Stägemann is doing nothing and Pourtalès has not answered. The rest is news of Napoleon, Paris, Murat and Württemberg. He asks for blank forms and wants Eberhard in Vienna for the settlement.

oe1bu9454-286.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna to Prince Hohenlohe during the Hundred Days. He comments on Napoleon's advance and says little can be done for now: Hardenberg promises, and Stägemann does as he pleases. Because the Prusimska has been given the Polish estates back, he has handed in a P.M. (286a). The P.M. works out the Prince's claims on the Kaemen and Trąbczyn estates, totalling 390100 rt, to be paid in cash or in estates. General Amstetten supports compensation in estates. Triebenfeld asks for a quick answer and blank sheets (Blanquets), and says Beguelin wants a letter from the Prince. A postscript dated 1 April covers politics again. The text is partly garbled, especially the passage on lines 36-47.

oe1bu9454-287.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna to the Prince. The Prince's letter of 3 April arrived unsealed inside the envelope to the Post Director. Triebenfeld welcomes Prinz Adolph's decision to join the army. He will ask the King, who is said to leave on the 18th, where Adolph should go and which uniform he should wear. He passed Lombardini's letter on through Beguelin but is holding back Hahn's threatening one. The letter then gives long political and military news: the Hortensia letter, troop numbers of the allies, Bonaparte outlawed. Pourtalès has not arrived, and Radziwiłł is going to Posen with Zerboni. oe1bu9454-291.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna to Prince Friedrich Ludwig. The Cabinets Ordre of 27 April orders prompt payment of 100000 rt to Fürst August; it was sent to Kircheisen and made known on 6 May. oe1bu9454-292.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Vienna to Prince Friedrich Ludwig. The compensation matter is recognised and now lies with the Kayser; Stein promises help and Hardenberg is to confirm in writing. In the Cosmar affair Stägemann defends Cosmar and wants everything referred to the Justice Minister. Triebenfeld argues before the Fürst Kanzler that Cosmar must deposit the sums fixed in the 1799 deed and the 1811 settlement at the Brieg court. oe1bu9454-295.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Posen to the Prince. His main plan has failed: the Russian Kaiser passed through Kalisz the night before he arrived. In Posen, Ober Post Director Espagne tells him that Staats Kanzler Hardenberg is still in Paris, will travel via Cassel and Frankfurt, and will reach Berlin only in about 3 weeks. Espagne also says Barbe is lying ill with nerve fever in Paris. Triebenfeld is looking into the Betsche (Pszczew) matter, where the subjects have asked for the contract to be cancelled. He then means to go to Blizanow for money from his tenant, and on to Berlin. He encloses Zerboni's answer to Schenck and doubts Zerboni's claimed report to Hardenberg. He adds news about Stein and rumours about Radziwiłł and Biron. Nothing on Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-298.notes: Triebenfeld, ill at Blizanow, P.M. to the Prince: forwards letters (Madame Schenck delayed messenger), illness continues; Zerboni's view; compensation secured via Vienna treaty, Boidelang to succeed Barbe, friend of Humboldt; Kaiser returns end of March, no hurry to Berlin; first affairs here, then Betsche, then Berlin. Missing letters; asks Strelitz post office to forward by express; stays till 15 Jan. Asks for game delivered to Faust at Gostyszyn. Prussian money devalued in Kalisz; Poles refuse troops against Turks (garbled). No Trąbczyn content.

claims.statement: Triebenfeld ist weiter krank.
Wegen der im Wiener Tractat zugesagten Entschädigung fürchtet er nichts, da Boidelang, sein Freund und Vertrauter Humboldts, an Barbes Stelle treten soll.
Er will erst hier aufräumen, dann die Angelegenheit in Pszczew ordnen, danach nach Berlin reisen.
Bitte, das Postamt Strelitz anzuweisen, Briefe durch Expresse zu schicken.
claims.why: Lines 31-34: the Strelitz post office is to hand all letters to the Fürst, and the Fürst is to send them on by express messenger. The post office does not send them to Triebenfeld itself.

oe1bu9454-299.notes: Triebenfeld writes to the Prince from Blizanow. He is over his illness but still weak. Main subject is Pszczew (Betsche): he wants to reach agreement with Leixner in Międzyrzecz about the receipt that has been found. The townspeople and peasants want the contract cancelled, and Zerboni wishes the same; Triebenfeld sets his conditions and works out what the Prince would receive (127000 Rthl, of which 99000 are still outstanding). He argues that the 72000 and 65000 Rthl charged on Pszczew belong on Kamionna. Also covered: Trzciński asks for a delay until Johanni; Schenck wants a general power of attorney, and Triebenfeld asks for a letter so he can be rid of him; the compensation business, with Minister Humboldt; Zerboni's household. Nothing on Trąbczyn.

claims.statement: Er will sich in Pszczew mit Leixner in Międzyrzecz einigen, die aufgefundene Quittung geltend machen und die Schuld im Hypothekenbuch löschen lassen.
Bürger und Bauern sowie Zerboni wünschen die Aufhebung des Kontrakts; Triebenfeld will nur unter Bedingungen zustimmen, darunter die Abführung von 11000 Rthl rückständigem Canon an den Fürsten.
Nach seiner Rechnung stehen dem Fürsten aus Pszczew noch 99000 Rthl zu.
Die auf Pszczew eingetragenen 72000 und 65000 Rthl gehören laut Quittung auf Kamionna.
claims.why: Lines 63-65 give this as what Triebenfeld insists on ('Ich bestehe darauf'), not as an established fact.

claims.statement: Trzciński hat um Aufschub bis Johanni gebeten und ihn erhalten.
Schenck will eine Generalvollmacht; Triebenfeld bittet den Fürsten um ein Schreiben, um ihn loszuwerden.

oe1bu9454-300.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Blizanow to the Prince. The upper left margin is damaged. First, something ("[...]schlag") has been left at Gostyszyn but no letter came with it, and he will send for it. Then Posen news: Zerboni and his secretary Schmidt drafted a report on organising the Grand Duchy of Posen. Fürst Radziwiłł refused to co-sign because it contradicted what the King had told him, and Zerboni answered "Ich bin hier regierender Herr". Radziwiłł left offended, his wife followed, and Z was sent to Berlin. Rumours from Petersburg: the Senate is said to have rejected the Polish constitution, and Grand Duke Constantin has hurried there. Plans: once his messenger is back from Schlawenschitz, he goes to Betsche and then to Berlin for the compensation business. Nothing on Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-301.notes: Triebenfeld writes from Blizanow to the Prince. He has received the Prince's letter of the 26th through Lombardini and sends congratulations for "the important day" (a birthday or name day). He has no new business to report beyond his earlier letters and asks for the Prince's decisions. Lombardini will report in person. Triebenfeld is waiting for his son and for a tenant for Schweinern (Świniary), and will then go to Posen and Betsche. He is hopeful about the compensation matter because he has won over Ober Prefect v Smiedecki in Kalisz. He suggests that game be sent, for here and for Zerboni in Posen, since the last delivery spoiled. Nothing about Trąbczyn.

oe1bu9454-302.notes: Triebenfeld to the Prince, from Kontop. He had Hawich (Justiz Bürgermeister of Zagorowo, now a Warsaw notary) and Ober-Inspektor Hecker with him and issued thirteen court powers of attorney. They cover: the Dąbska and the Trąbczyn estates, lifting the sequestration, interest payments, a suit against Oppenheimer et Wolf, removing the sequester Honrichs, Niedźwiecki's rent arrears, purchase-money arrears, the Olesnicer hereditary tenants, boundary suits, the Reichstag, the Invaliden Casse and the heirs' arrears. Schenck of Neusatz recorded them. The parallel copy (doc 48) differs in a few places: Abweisung, 23000, Radzinskischen, Lahrschen.

oe1bu9454-303.notes: This is not a letter but a table: an extract from the Fürstlich Hohenlohe liquidation protocols listing 142 capital claims, each with its sum in Gold or Courant. The total is 17,874 Rthl Gold and 1,414,377 Rthl 7 g 11 d Courant. Among the largest claims are Carl v Stoessel, Goldstücker, the Stoessel curator, Hein in Breslau, Charlotte von Triebenfeld, Koppan, Barnheim, the Köckritz heirs and the Sobottendorff heirs. Many names are garbled. There is no reference to Trąbczyn. No sender, recipient or date is given.
